{{Short description|Statistical test}}

The '''Ljung–Box test''' (named for [[Greta M. Ljung]] and [[George E. P. Box]]) is a type of [[statistical test]] of whether any of a group of [[autocorrelation]]s of a [[time series]] are different from zero. Instead of testing [[randomness]] at each distinct lag, it tests the "overall" randomness based on a number of lags, and is therefore a [[portmanteau test]].

This test is sometimes known as the '''Ljung–Box Q test''', and it is closely connected to the '''Box–Pierce test''' (which is named after [[George E. P. Box]] and David A. Pierce). In fact, the Ljung–Box test statistic was described explicitly in the paper that led to the use of the Box–Pierce statistic,<ref name=BP/><ref name=LB/> and from which that statistic takes its name. The Box–Pierce test statistic is a simplified version of the Ljung–Box statistic for which subsequent simulation studies have shown poor performance.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Davies|first1=Neville|last2=Newbold|first2=Paul|date=1979|title=Some power studies of a portmanteau test of time series model specification.|url=https://academic.oup.com/biomet/article-abstract/66/1/153/223702|journal=Biometrika|volume=66|issue=1|pages=153–155|doi=10.1093/biomet/66.1.153|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

The Ljung–Box test is widely applied in [[econometrics]] and other applications of [[time series analysis]]. A similar assessment can be also carried out with the [[Breusch–Godfrey test]] and the [[Durbin–Watson statistic|Durbin–Watson test]].

==Formal definition==
The Ljung–Box test may be defined as:
: '''<math>H_0</math>:''' The data is not correlated (i.e. the correlations in the population from which the sample is taken are 0, so that any observed correlations in the data result from randomness of the sampling process).
: '''<math>H_a</math>:''' The data exhibit serial correlation.

The test statistic is:<ref name=LB/>
:<math>
Q = n(n+2)\sum_{k=1}^h\frac{\hat{\rho}^2_k}{n-k}
</math>
where ''n'' is the sample size, <math>\hat{\rho}_k</math> is the sample autocorrelation at lag ''k'', and ''h'' is the number of lags being tested. Under <math>H_0</math> the statistic Q asymptotically follows a <math>\chi^2_{(h)}</math>. For [[significance level]] α, the [[critical region]] for rejection of the hypothesis of randomness is:

: <math>
Q > \chi_{1-\alpha,h}^2
</math>

where <math>\chi_{1-\alpha,h}^2</math> is the (1&nbsp;−&nbsp;''α'')-[[quantile]]<ref>{{Cite book|title=Introduction to Time Series and Forecasting|url=https://archive.org/details/introductiontoti00broc|url-access=limited|isbn=978-0-387-95351-9|page=[https://archive.org/details/introductiontoti00broc/page/n49 36]|last1=Brockwell|first1=Peter J.|last2=Davis|first2=Richard A.|last3=Davis|first3=R. J.|date=2002-03-08|publisher=Taylor & Francis }}</ref> of the [[chi-squared distribution]] with ''h'' degrees of freedom.

The Ljung–Box test is commonly used in [[autoregressive integrated moving average]] (ARIMA) modeling. Note that it is applied to the [[errors and residuals in statistics|residuals]] of a fitted ARIMA model, not the original series, and in such applications the hypothesis actually being tested is that the residuals from the ARIMA model have no autocorrelation. When testing the residuals of an estimated ARIMA model, the degrees of freedom need to be adjusted to reflect the parameter estimation. For example, for an ARIMA(''p'',0,''q'') model, the degrees of freedom should be set to <math>h - p - q</math>.<ref>{{cite book |last=Davidson |first=James |title=Econometric Theory |year=2000 |publisher=Blackwell |isbn=978-0-631-21584-4 |page=162 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=shWtvsFbxlkC&pg=PA162 }}</ref>

==Box–Pierce test==
The Box–Pierce test uses the test statistic, in the notation outlined above, given by<ref name=BP/>
:<math>
Q_\text{BP} = n \sum_{k=1}^h \hat{\rho}^2_k,
</math>
and it uses the same critical region as defined above.

Simulation studies have shown that the distribution for the Ljung–Box statistic is closer to a <math>\chi^2_{(h)}</math> distribution than is the distribution for the Box–Pierce statistic for all sample sizes including small ones.{{Citation needed|date=June 2011}}

== Implementations in statistics packages ==
* [[R (programming language)|R]]: the <code>Box.test</code> function in the stats package<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/box.test.html|title=R: Box–Pierce and Ljung–Box Tests|website=stat.ethz.ch|access-date=2016-06-05}}</ref>
* [[Python (programming language)|Python]]: the <code>acorr_ljungbox</code> function in the <code>statsmodels</code> package<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.statsmodels.org/dev/generated/statsmodels.stats.diagnostic.acorr_ljungbox.html|title=Python: Ljung–Box Tests|website=statsmodels.org|access-date=2018-07-23}}</ref>
* [[Julia (programming language)|Julia]]: the Ljung–Box tests and the Box–Pierce tests in the ''<code>HypothesisTests</code>'' package<ref>{{cite web|url=https://juliastats.org/HypothesisTests.jl/latest/time_series/ |title= Time series tests |website=juliastats.org |access-date=2020-02-04}}</ref>
* [[SPSS]]: the Box-Ljung statistic is included by default in output produced by the IBM SPSS Statistics Forecasting module.
